Report Verbs and Impersonal Passive Constructions
When you report beliefs and information that other people have, you can use report verbs such as think, claim, mention, request and point out.
You often use these report verbs with impersonal passive constructions. These are types of sentences that don't refer to any person or thing specifically.
It's thought that the CEO earns too much money.
You can introduce a statement with impersonal references such as They say, think, believe ... or It is said, thought, believed ...
It's thought that CEOs make too much money. (= CEOs are believed to make too much money).

How to Add Visuals to a Presentation
Visuals can support your presentation, but it is important to know how to use them effectively.
Here are some tips to keep in mind when adding visuals to your presentation at work:

• Be consistent with color and font size. Having too much variety can make you appear disjointed and can be distracting for your audience. Match the color with the tone of your presentation (lively or conservative).
  • Consider the culture of the people you are presenting to. Avoid any images or font colors that may be offensive to others.
  • Use images in a memorable way. Choose images that tell a story and that help your audience remember them.
  • If you have a lot of information, break it down into smaller points. Do not overwhelm your audience.
  • Keep your slides simple and clean.

images.text:
PowerPoint presentations are a great way to support a speech in order to focus attention on a subject. However, a bad presentation can lead to the opposite result, because of poor design choices.  Following these suggestions will be useful for avoiding the most common mistakes.
It has been claimed that presentations should be very appealing to look at. However, it has not been mentioned as much that the messages on your page, either through words, images or illustrations, are much more important than anything else. In reality, each slide should be very basic and simple owing to our limited attention spans.

Secondly, it has been pointed out that it is important to be consistent in your choices. You should use the same font face and sizes on all slides. Presenters are often requested to use a font size that is large enough to read from a distance. If you want to play with colors, always keep contrast in mind so as to ensure that the text is easy to read. If you use your company logo, choose contrasting colors for other elements on the slide. A poor choice of colors can shatter a presentation due to unattractive combinations. If you're unsure which colors match best, you can find a website to get a set of matching colors.

Thirdly, when you are drafting your message, remember the golden rule: KIS (Keep It Simple). Images are key elements of every presentation. They say that a picture is worth a thousand words. Your audience wants to have a visual representation of what you're talking about in order to better understand your message. You should be talking freely, not reading your text. The tendency to read all the words on a slide is so common that most presenters only use keywords. Whether you are describing your data or explaining circumstances, you'll want to tell a story. That's how the human brain works.
